C005.subject: Remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote work office work]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled experiment comparing deep-focus task completion times between remote workers with dedicated home offices (using screen monitoring) and in-office workers in a quiet environment. — Directly tests the core condition (dedicated space + monitoring) and scope (deep focus) against office baseline, providing causal evidence.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on productivity effects of remote vs. office work, specifically filtering for studies that control for home office quality and use of monitoring software. — Synthesizes available evidence to assess whether the conditional claim is supported across multiple contexts, addressing the disputed status.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model of attention and interruption costs in remote vs. office environments, incorporating monitoring as a deterrent to non-work activities. — Provides a mechanistic explanation for why the condition might increase productivity, allowing prediction of boundary conditions (e.g., task complexity, monitoring intrusiveness).

scope.domain: tasks requiring deep focus and minimal interruption

qualifier.condition: when employees have dedicated home office spaces and are required to use real-time screen monitoring software

C006.subject: Office work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Office work remote work]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled field experiment comparing productivity on deep-focus tasks (e.g., coding, writing, data analysis) in urban office vs. home settings during weekday business hours, with objective output metrics (e.g., lines of code, word count, error rates). — Directly tests the hypothesis under the specified scope (deep focus, minimal interruption) and qualifiers (urban office with high-speed internet, weekday hours), providing causal evidence on productivity differences.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of existing studies on office vs. remote work productivity, focusing on tasks requiring sustained attention and low interruption. — Synthesizes available evidence to assess the overall effect size and consistency across studies, addressing the disputed status and moderate confidence level.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model of distraction and cognitive load in office vs. remote environments, incorporating factors like ambient noise, social interruptions, and self-regulation. — Provides a framework to predict conditions under which office work might outperform remote work for deep-focus tasks, guiding further empirical tests and explaining potential moderators.

scope.domain: tasks requiring deep focus and minimal interruption

qualifier.temporal: during standard business hours on weekdays
qualifier.geographic: in urban office environments with high-speed internet access

C011.subject: Productivity gains from remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Productivity gains from remote work increased burnout and communication delays]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal field study comparing productivity metrics (e.g., output per hour, project completion rates) and burnout indicators (e.g., Maslach Burnout Inventory scores) in fully remote vs. hybrid teams over 18+ months. — Directly tests the hypothesis that initial productivity gains are offset by burnout and delays beyond 12 months, using objective and subjective measures in a real-world setting.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on remote work productivity, burnout, and communication delays, focusing on studies with observation periods >12 months. — Synthesizes available evidence to determine whether the net effect of remote work on long-term organizational performance is positive, neutral, or negative, accounting for variations in context and methodology.

[PATH:theoretical] Agent-based simulation modeling the dynamics of remote work: productivity, communication network efficiency, and cumulative burnout over time, parameterized with empirical data from prior studies. — Allows testing of causal mechanisms and long-term trajectories under controlled assumptions, revealing conditions under which productivity gains are negated or sustained beyond 12 months.

C012.subject: Remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote work long-term productivity and employee well-being]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal employer-employee panel data from multinational knowledge firms (e.g., Microsoft, GitLab) tracking productivity metrics (e.g., output per hour, project completion rates) and well-being indicators (e.g., burnout scales, retention) over 2+ years, pre- and post-mandate changes. — Directly tests the causal link between remote work and sustained productivity/well-being using real-world, time-series data, controlling for confounding factors like industry shocks.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of peer-reviewed studies (2020–2025) on remote work, focusing on long-term outcomes (≥2 years) in knowledge-economy sectors, including effect sizes for productivity and well-being. — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess overall direction and strength of the relationship, identifying moderators (e.g., autonomy, team cohesion) that explain conflicting findings.

[PATH:empirical] Natural experiment comparing firms that switched to permanent remote vs. hybrid vs. in-office policies post-2020, using administrative data (e.g., HR records, performance reviews) and employee surveys over 3+ years. — Leverages exogenous policy variation to isolate causal effects, addressing selection bias and capturing long-term adaptation effects often missed in short-term studies.

qualifier.temporal: post-2020, longitudinal studies spanning at least two years
